objective.statement: Write chromatic scales with correct spelling, and judge written ones.
successCriteria: I know a chromatic scale moves only by semitones.
I know every letter name is used once or twice, never three times, and none is missing.
I can write a correct chromatic scale up or down from any starting note.

explanation.text: A chromatic scale is made entirely of semitones. Over one octave it contains every note: thirteen notes counting both ends. The hard part is not finding the notes but naming them. The same black key can be a sharp or a flat, and a scale must be spelt so that it is easy to read.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with thirteen semibreves: a chromatic scale from C to C, going up, with sharps.

explanation.caption: Chromatic scale from C, ascending, using sharps.

explanation.text: There is no single correct spelling. These are the rules for a good one: move by a semitone each time; use every letter name at least once, and no letter more than twice; and do not use more accidentals than you need. Going up it is usual to use sharps for the black keys, and coming down flats, but any spelling that follows the rules is right.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with thirteen semibreves: a chromatic scale from C down to C, with flats.

explanation.caption: Chromatic scale from C, descending, using flats.

explanation.text: Check a scale like this: (1) is every step a semitone? (2) is each letter used once or twice, with none missing? (3) are there double accidentals you do not need? A scale such as C, C♯, D♭, D ... fails at once: C♯ and D♭ are the same sound, so that step is not a semitone.
Semitones only. Every letter once or twice. No double accidentals. Sharps going up and flats coming down is the usual choice, but any spelling that follows the rules is correct.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with six semibreves from E up to A: E, F, F sharp, G, G sharp, A.

steps: Play every key from E to A, white and black: each step is a semitone.
E to F and F♯ to G are already semitones; the black keys fill in the tones.
Name the black keys with sharps going up.
demonstration.textAlternative: The start of a chromatic scale from E.

mastery.completion: The lesson is complete when every step has been answered correctly (retries allowed). Only first-attempt, hint-free independent answers count as mastery evidence; guided steps never do.

provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 12 and First Steps Grade 4 section 12 (pp. 97-99, read in the PDF): a chromatic scale is all semitones; 'at least one note on every line and every space, but not more than two'; unnecessary accidentals; key-signature preferences. The book says harmonic and melodic chromatic forms are not required. The grader accepts every spelling that satisfies the letter and semitone rules (tested), not one fixed sequence. Questions give no key signature; the book's preference for the notes of a key signature is mentioned but not examined (TEACHER TO CONFIRM).
